summary: Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions (RAMS) lets a receiver quickly start consuming a multicast stream by first getting data via a unicast retransmission session. This informational RFC covers deployment considerations.

eli5.summary: When you switch to a TV channel, you want it right away. This describes how to get a quick start before joining the main broadcast.

questions: how to speed up multicast channel changes
how to deploy rams with multiple streams
when to use different multicast groups for fec
subtitle: Practical deployment scenarios for rapid multicast stream acquisition.

tldr.problem: When joining a multicast stream, receivers want to start consuming data immediately, but may miss reference information at the stream start.
tldr.mechanism: RAMS provides a unicast retransmission session that rapidly feeds the receiver key data before or alongside joining the main multicast stream, enabling fast channel changes.
tldr.outcome: Receivers can quickly acquire multicast content, but deploying RAMS with multiple streams requires careful coordination of feedback targets and bandwidth allocation.

today: RFC 6659 is an Informational document that provides deployment guidance for RFC 6285 (RAMS). It has not been obsoleted and serves as a practical reference for operators deploying rapid multicast acquisition in real networks.

sections.title: What RAMS Is
sections.content: The Rapid Acquisition of Multicast RTP Sessions (RAMS) method, defined in RFC 6285, lets a receiver quickly start consuming a multicast RTP stream. When a receiver joins a multicast group, it may not have the initial packets, so it joins a temporary unicast retransmission session with a dedicated server. The retransmission server rapidly sends key reference data—often at an accelerated rate—until the receiver is caught up, then the receiver switches to the regular multicast stream. This process is transparent to the application and transparent to the main multicast stream.
sections.eli5: When you turn on the TV, the helper gives you the important bits real fast so you are not waiting to see the show.

sections.title: Core Concepts
sections.content:
RAMS deployment involves several key concepts. An SSM session (Source-Specific Multicast) is identified by a source address and a multicast group; each SSM session can have only one feedback target (a unique address and port combination). An SSM session can carry one or more RTP streams, identified by their SSRC (Synchronization Source). Streams can be multiplexed at the SSRC level within a single RTP session, or at the session level in different UDP flows.

The RFC distinguishes between different clock rates: when two RTP streams have different clock rates, they must use different SSRCs or be carried in different RTP sessions, since the sequence numbering and clock information are tied to the SSRC.
sections.eli5: Each stream needs its own label (SSRC), and all streams in a group talk to the same feedback address. If streams tick at different speeds, they need different labels.

sections.title: Four Deployment Patterns
sections.content: The RFC presents four real-world scenarios. Scenario #1: Two Multicast Groups carries primary and FEC (Forward Error Correction) streams over different multicast groups, each with a different feedback target. This allows parallel RAMS sessions to run independently. Scenario #2: One Multicast Group carries multiple streams (for example, video and audio) to the same multicast group but different destination ports, sharing a single feedback target and SSM session. Scenario #3: SSRC Multiplexing carries multiple streams to the same multicast group and port, identified by different SSRCs within a single RTP session. Scenario #4: Payload-Type Multiplexing places different payload types in the same RTP stream; while permissible, this approach is not recommended because it shares sequence numbering and prevents RAMS from operating per payload type.
sections.eli5: Different ways to split the streams: separate channels, same channel different ports, same channel same port but different labels, or mixing everything in one stream (not recommended).

sections.title: Feedback Targets and Signaling
sections.content: When a receiver wants to acquire multiple streams, each RAMS request goes to a feedback target with a specific SSRC identifier. A critical constraint is that each unique feedback target can be associated with at most one RTP session. This is why in Scenario #2, streams within the same SSM session must have unique SSRC values: the receiver uses SSRC to tell the feedback target which stream it wants to acquire. In Scenario #1, where streams are in different SSM sessions, the SSRC values need not be unique across sessions because each session has its own feedback target. The SSRC values can be signaled in the Session Description Protocol (SDP) or learned from the RTP stream itself; however, RAMS requires out-of-band signaling (SDP) so the feedback target can identify the stream before packets arrive.
sections.eli5: Each helper knows which stream you asked for because you tell it the stream's label. If multiple streams share one helper, they need different labels.

sections.title: Forward Error Correction and Bandwidth
sections.content: When primary and FEC streams are acquired together, the receiver has limited bandwidth to split between them. In Scenario #1, where FEC is in a separate multicast group, the receiver can focus all available bandwidth on the primary stream during RAMS, then join the FEC stream afterward, or allocate bandwidth between both RAMS sessions. In Scenario #2, where primary and FEC share a multicast group but use different ports, the receiver can request all available bandwidth for the primary stream alone, but must account for the FEC stream's bandwidth once it joins the multicast group. In Scenario #3, both streams use the same port and SSM session, so bandwidth must be pre-allocated between them. The receiver can update the Max Receive Bitrate during the acquisition, though changing it mid-session is error-prone. All scenarios require careful advance planning to avoid temporary network congestion during the accelerated burst.
sections.eli5: The helper sends you two things at once (video and error-fixing stuff), you have to share your download speed between them smartly, or get one first then the other.
